lead: A guidance law gives an acceleration command. Something physical must turn it into a sideways force: the airframe, its fins, and the small servo behind each fin. This chapter covers the missile body, the three ways to steer it — aerodynamic fins, thrust vector or reaction jets, and skid-to-turn versus bank-to-turn — and the fin actuation chain that turns milliamps of command into hundreds of newtons of rod force. Every homing missile is built around this chain. Only a few universities teach this depth.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 for hydraulic and pneumatic supply, Unit 3 for actuators, and Chapter 6.5 for the acceleration command.

blocks.text: A missile airframe has a nose dome that lets the seeker look out, a body carrying the motor and warhead, and fins. Fins near the nose are canards; tail fins are the more common choice. Both make lift.

Lift comes from two sources. The body makes lift when it flies at an angle of attack α, the angle between the body axis and the airflow. The fins add lift in proportion to their deflection δ, the angle between fin and body.

blocks.where: L is lift in newtons; q = ½ρv² is dynamic pressure in pascals, with ρ the air density in kg/m³ and v the speed in m/s; S is a reference area in m²; C_L is the dimensionless lift coefficient. At v = 0 the fins do nothing.

blocks.text: Propulsion, briefly: a solid rocket motor for short range, a ramjet for long cruise, and thrust vector control during boost while speed is still low.

sections.h3: Control types and the turn convention

blocks.text: Aerodynamic fin control works inside the atmosphere, where q is high enough for useful lift and hinge moment.

Thrust vector control (TVC) tilts the motor thrust itself; reaction jets at nose or tail push the body directly. Both work outside the atmosphere, where q ≈ 0 and fins are dead weight, and during boost.

Skid-to-turn (STT) pitches and yaws the body independently with two fin pairs, without rolling. It is quick and suits a cruciform airframe. Bank-to-turn (BTT) rolls the missile first so its lift vector lies in the turn plane, then pulls one elevator. BTT gives more lift per degree of angle of attack and keeps a ramjet inlet in clean flow, but the roll costs time. See Chapter 6.7.

Three technologies: electric, where a brushless motor drives the fin through a gearbox — clean but moderate torque; electro-hydraulic, where a pump or accumulator supplies oil and a servo valve meters it into a ram — highest torque for its size, used on large fins; pneumatic, where hot gas from a gas generator drives the ram — cheap and short-lived.

items: Acceleration command arrives from the autopilot.
Servo amplifier takes voltage in and gives current out.
Torque motor moves the servo valve flapper.
Valve meters oil into the ram; the push rod moves.
Position sensor on the fin feeds deflection back to the amplifier.

blocks.text: Two limits set the response. Torque limit is the largest hinge torque the actuator can hold; it caps deflection at high q. Rate limit is the largest slew rate in °/s; it caps how fast the fin arrives. A rate-limited servo answers a step with a ramp.

The actuator must beat the hinge moment — the aerodynamic torque on the fin about its hinge — plus inertia and friction. Gyros (rate, free, dynamically tuned) sense the resulting motion; their physics is in Unit 5.

examples.question: A fin needs 30 N·m of hinge torque and must slew 2° in 20 ms. The push rod acts 25 mm from the hinge. Find the rod force, the slew rate in °/s and rad/s, and the actuator power.
steps: Rod force F = torque ÷ r = 30 ÷ 0.025 = 1200 N.
examples.answer: Rod force 1200 N, slew rate 100 °/s (1.745 rad/s), actuator power 52.4 W.
examples.check:
T = 30.0
r = 0.025
angle = 2.0
t = 0.02
F = T / r
deg = angle / t
rad = deg * 3.141592653589793 / 180
P = T * rad
print(round(F, 1))
print(round(deg, 1))
print(round(rad, 3))
print(round(P, 1))

traps: Hinge moment is the aerodynamic torque on the fin; actuator torque is what the servo supplies. Dropping the lever arm turns 30 N·m into a wrong 30 N.
Power needs rad/s. Using 100 °/s gives 3000 W, 57 times too large.
A torque-limited servo saturates and lags; a rate-limited servo ramps. Different step responses, and examiners ask which you have.
Fins cannot steer at launch because q ≈ 0. That phase belongs to TVC or reaction jets.
STT does not roll the airframe; BTT does.

quiz.q: Name the three fin actuation technologies.

quiz.a: The aerodynamic torque on a fin about its hinge line.

quiz.q: Why are fins useless during boost?
quiz.a: Speed and hence q = ½ρv² are low, so fin lift and hinge moment are small; TVC is used.

quiz.q: A fin needs 18 N·m and the rod acts at 30 mm. Find the rod force.
A servo is rate-limited at 100 °/s and gets a 10° step. Describe the fin response and its effect on the loop.
quiz.a: The fin ramps for 0.1 s, then holds. The added 0.1 s lag cuts phase margin and can destabilise a high-gain autopilot.

quiz.q: Why does an electro-hydraulic servo suit a large fin better than an electric one?
quiz.a: Oil pressure gives high torque in a small ram volume; a motor of the same mass gives less torque.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production missiles are moving to all-electric fin actuation: high-torque brushless motors with harmonic drives remove hydraulic fluid, which is heavy and hard to maintain in the field. Reaction-jet control is being revisited for exo-atmospheric interceptors, where fins do nothing. Search 'electromechanical actuator missile fin' and 'bank-to-turn autopilot design' to go further.
